item.title: Defining A New Secular — Mon Nov 9, 5:30 PM — None
item.description: The Islamic Secular argues that the common notion of a fundamental conflict between the secular and the religious cannot be applied to Islam. This is not because Islam rejects the secular in favor of the religious; it is because Islam's concept of the religious includes the secular. This is what is captured by the term "Islamic Secular." Contrary to both the notion that "religion" in Islam equals "sharī'ah," and to the concomitant notion that sharī'ah is the all-encompassing, exclusive metric of assessment in Islam, this book argues that, while Islam is all-encompassing, sharī'ah is bounded. This leaves a space between the limited circumference of sharī'ah and the unlimited circumference of Islam. While both spaces are "religious" in that they come under the adjudicative gaze of the God of Islam, only the shar'ī space draws directly upon sharī'ah and its sources, while the non-shar'ī space does not. item.title: My Friend Abe - Holocaust Survivor Abe Piasek's Story — Mon Nov 9, 6:30 PM — French Family Science Center 2231
item.description:

Abe was taken from his family in Poland at age 13 in 1942 (he never saw his parents or little sister again) and forced to work in three slave labor camps over the next three years. Abe's story will be presented by Steve Goldberg, Duke grad, history teacher, lawyer, and friend of Abe's. Steve has shared Abe's incredible and inspiring story over 220 times. For more details, visit MyFriendAbe.com.

item.title: Elvira Notari: Oltre il silenzio – Film Screening and Discussion with Director Valerio Ciriaci — Mon Nov 9, 7:00 PM — None
item.description:
Join us for a screening of Elvira Notari: Oltre il silenzio (Awen Films, 2025), presented at the 82nd Venice International Film Festival, followed by a conversation with director Valerio Ciriaci.
Elvira Notari was Italy's first woman film director. From her studio in Naples, Dora Film, she wrote, directed and produced dozens of feature films in the 1910s and 1920s: popular melodramas shot in the streets of the city, with a realism that anticipated later Italian cinema. Most of her work has been lost, and her name was nearly erased from film history. Ciriaci's documentary follows the traces she left behind and asks what it means to recover a filmmaker from silence.
Introductions by Hank Okazaki and Tania Rispoli. Discussion to follow with Tom Whiteside (Director of Durham Cinematheque) and Roberto Dainotto (Professor of Literature).
Co-sponsored by Cinematic Arts and the Center for Documentary Studies; Italian Language Program; Romance Studies; Franklin Humanities Institute; History,

The Daily Planet Café is open 5–8pm with a full menu during the Science Café. Join us in-person or watch the livestream on YouTube. Tonight’s Topic In Sri Lanka’s North Central Province, expanding agriculture is increasing overlap between human settlements and elephant habitat. Elephants that forage on farm crops face retaliation from farmers protecting their livelihoods, making Human-Elephant Conflict (HEC) one of the region’s most pressing conservation challenges. Yet not all elephants engage in crop raiding, and little is known about the characteristics that influence the likelihood of crop raiding. item.title: Community Stories: Sustaining North Carolina’s Black Heritage — Fri Feb 5, 10:00 AM — Gregg Museum of Art & Design
item.description:
Community Stories: Sustaining North Carolina’s Black Heritage at the Gregg Museum of Art & Design presents a series of vignettes exploring spaces of dignity, belonging, safety, and imagination within Black communities across North Carolina. Featuring historical photographs, contemporary images, artworks from the Gregg Museum collection including a handmade guitar by Freeman Vines, and ephemera from community partners, the exhibition reflects on place, memory, creativity, and spiritual resilience across generations. Through stories of triumph and adversity, Community Stories honors the ways Black Americans have sustained and uplifted their communities through family, entrepreneurship, cultural expression, and soulful imagination, while inspiring future generations.
Source: NC Cultural Resources

item.title: Mecklenburg's Declaration: NC's Revolutionary Presbyterians — Sat Feb 6 — Presbyterian Heritage Center
item.description:
An article published in the April 30, 1819 edition of the Raleigh Register and North Carolina Gazette proclaimed the following: “It is not probably known to many of our readers, that the citizens of Mecklenburg County, in this State, made a Declaration of Independence more than a year before Congress made theirs. The following Document on the subject has lately come to the hands of the Editor from unquestionable authority, and is published that it may go down to posterity.”
The document in question was called the Mecklenburg Declaration of Independence, and it had allegedly declared Mecklenburg “free and independent” from British rule on May 20, 1775. Of the 27 men who were said to have signed the document, almost all were Presbyterian.
But many people were confused – why were they just now hearing about this revolutionary action? The original document burned in a house fire in 1800, and the published version had been reconstructed from notes made by the clerk of the 1775 meeting.

item.title: Embodied Neuromechanics or: How I Learned to Stop Worrying and Love NeuroAI — Mon Nov 9, 12:00 PM — None
item.description:
Behavior is the ultimate output of the nervous system, but it has long resisted precise measurement. My lab develops AI tools, including SLEAP, that extract detailed body kinematics from video at scale, turning behavior into quantitative data on par with neural recordings and connectomes. We then use these measurements to build embodied neuromechanical models: artificial neural networks that control physically simulated animal bodies, linking neural circuits, biomechanics, and behavior in a single framework. Because these models are generative, they can simulate perturbations and produce mechanistic hypotheses that can be tested directly at the bench, creating a feedback loop between AI and experimental neuroscience.

item.title: On Reproductive Liberty — Mon Nov 9, 5:00 PM — East Duke Parlors
item.description:
This talk interrogates how slavery animates the psychic counters of abortion concerns. From the use of the Civil War as a metaphor for battles over personhood by abortion legal scholars such as Mary Ziegler to the constitutional originalism espoused by Justice Samuel Alito's reading of the fourteenth amendment in Dobbs, slavery occupies a foundational psychic landscape with the rhetorical strategies of abortion battles. To trace this emergence, this talk returns to nineteenth century medical jurisprudence to consider how the concept of portio viscerum matris situates gestation as the dividing line between the status of life and the conditions of property.

item.title: Primer to Causal Inference Workshop — Mon Nov 9, 5:00 PM — Bostock Library
item.description:
As ice cream consumption increases, so do shark attacks, but does eating ice cream really cause shark attacks? This example shows how two things can be related without one causing the other. Yet, in research, figuring out whether we can make a causal claim about the relationship between two variables isn't always so simple. This workshop introduces the basics of causal inference and helps you think more carefully about the claims you make as a researcher.
By the end of the workshop, you'll have a better understanding of how to: ~Identify what's needed to establish causality. ~Explore simple experimental and quasi-experimental approaches to studying cause and effect. ~Develop your own causal research questions.
If you want to move beyond identifying relationships and start exploring cause and effect, join us for this workshop.
